text.en: Asha read about a man in a simple dhoti who led millions with truth. "Gandhi," said the teacher.

Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and led the freedom movement on the principles of truth and non-violence (satyagraha). He led the Champaran and Kheda satyagrahas and the Ahmedabad mill strike.
He launched the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920 after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919 and the Rowlatt Act. It was called off after Chauri Chaura. The Civil Disobedience Movement began in 1930 with the Salt March to Dandi.
The Quit India Movement of 1942 called for 'Do or Die'. Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Indian National Army. India became independent on 15 August 1947.

It was called off after Chauri Chaura.
The Civil Disobedience Movement began in 1930 with the Salt March to Dandi.

Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Indian National Army.
India became independent on 15 August 1947.
Returning from twenty-one years in South Africa in 1915, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi transformed Indian nationalism into a peaceful, fearless mass movement.
Satyagraha meant 'truth-force' + Ahimsa (non-violence)—challenging injustice openly without hatred, beginning with three local victories in 1917–1918.
At Champaran (1917) he freed Bihar peasants from forced indigo farming; at Ahmedabad (1918) he backed textile workers; at Kheda (1918) he won tax relief after crop failure.

In 1919 Britain passed the oppressive Rowlatt Act allowing jail without trial; protests erupted nationwide until General Dyer ordered troops to shoot unarmed crowds at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919.
Rabindranath Tagore renounced his Knighthood in protest, and Gandhi joined the Khilafat Movement with Ali Brothers to forge Hindu–Muslim unity.
From 1920 to 1922, the Non-Cooperation Movement saw students leave British schools, lawyers like C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru quit courts, and homespun Khadi replace foreign cloth.
When protesters tragically burned a police station at Chauri Chaura in February 1922 killing 22 policemen, Gandhi halted the movement to preserve non-violence.
Next, Swarajists (C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru) entered legislatures to oppose bills from within, while revolutionaries—Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev and Chandrasekhar Azad—inspired youth.
In 1928, the all-white Simon Commission arrived with zero Indian members, greeted everywhere by black flags and cries of 'Simon Go Back!'—during which Lala Lajpat Rai was fatally injured.

board.text: 1928: Simon Go Back! & Lahore Purna Swaraj

text.en: At the December 1929 Lahore Congress, Jawaharlal Nehru raised the tricolour and declared 'Purna Swaraj' (Complete Independence), celebrating 26 January 1930 as Independence Day.
On 12 March 1930, Gandhi walked 241 miles from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi coastal sands in 24 days, picking up natural salt to launch Civil Disobedience.
Across India—from Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Red Shirts in the Northwest to Rajaji's Vedaranyam march in Tamil Nadu—millions peacefully broke unjust salt and forest laws.

board.text: Civil Disobedience sweeps coast to frontier

text.en: Following the 1931 Gandhi–Irwin Pact, Round Table Talks in London, and Dr B. R. Ambedkar's push for depressed-class rights resulting in the 1932 Poona Pact, social equality gained strength.
When World War II broke out in 1939 without consulting India, Congress ministries resigned and Socialists like Jayaprakash Narayan and farmers' Kisan Sabhas stepped forward.
Following the failed 1942 Cripps Mission, Gandhi thundered at Bombay on 8 August 1942: 'Quit India! Do or Die!'
Even with top leaders jailed overnight, citizens—guided underground by Aruna Asaf Ali and Usha Mehta's secret radio—paralysed British rule.
Abroad, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose led the Azad Hind Government in Singapore, inspiring the Indian National Army ('Delhi Chalo') with Captain Lakshmi Sahgal's Rani Jhansi Regiment.
After 1946 Royal Indian Navy ratings mutinied and the Cabinet Mission held talks, Britain realised India could no longer be ruled.
On 15 August 1947, amid the sorrow of Partition, India won independence and Jawaharlal Nehru delivered 'Tryst with Destiny'.
Notice how every section of society joined: farmers, mill workers, Dalit leaders, women, youth and soldiers.
Follow the milestones: 1917 Champaran -> 1920 Non-Cooperation -> 1930 Salt March -> 1942 Quit India -> 1947 Freedom.
Gandhi's phase proved that courageous ordinary people united in non-violent discipline can topple the mightiest empire.

problem.en: Why did Mahatma Gandhi choose salt as the symbol to launch the 1930 Civil Disobedience Movement?

text.en: Spot its everyday necessity.

why.en: Rich or poor, Hindu, Muslim or Christian—every household needed daily salt, making the British monopoly tax hurt the poorest families.

text.en: Spot its non-violent power.

why.en: Making natural salt from seawater peacefully defied the British government without injuring anyone.

text.en: See the nationwide wave.

why.en: One simple pinch of Dandi salt sparked mass marches across India, including Rajaji's Vedaranyam march in Tamil Nadu.
